terms.def: A team activity where you argue about whether a big change should happen.
terms.plain: In policy debate, two teams of two students face off over a single yearly question about U.S. government policy. One team proposes a specific change (a plan) and the other team argues against it. It's part debate, part research project, and part strategy game.
terms.example: This year's topic is national health insurance. The Affirmative might argue the U.S. should pass Medicare for All. The Negative argues that plan will make things worse — or that a different fix would work better.
terms.where: The whole activity — every round, every tournament.
terms.watch: Policy debate isn't about your personal opinion. You argue whichever side you're assigned, using evidence — not feelings.

terms.def: The big topic that the whole country debates for the entire year.
terms.plain: The resolution is one sentence, chosen by the national debate community, that sets the topic for the whole school year. Every round in the country debates the same resolution. The Affirmative has to defend a plan that fits inside it.
terms.example: The 2026–2027 resolution: "The United States federal government should establish national health insurance in the United States."
terms.where: Written at the top of every 1AC. Referenced constantly in Topicality debates.
terms.watch: The resolution stays the same all year — don't waste time arguing whether it's a good topic. Argue the plan.

terms.def: The team that says: "YES, this change should happen."
terms.plain: The Affirmative team proposes a specific plan that fits the resolution and defends it as a good idea. They give the first speech of the round (the 1AC) and the last speech (the 2AR). They carry the burden of proving the plan is worth doing.
terms.example: On the health insurance topic, an Affirmative team might defend Medicare for All, a public option, or coverage for undocumented immigrants.
terms.where: AFF speaks first (1AC), last (2AR), and gets speeches 1, 3, 5, and 7 out of 8.
terms.watch: You don't have to defend all possible plans — just YOUR specific plan. Don't let the NEG stretch you to defend things you never proposed.

terms.def: The team that says: "NO, that change is a bad idea, or it won't work."
terms.plain: The Negative team argues against the Affirmative's specific plan. They don't have to defend the way things are now — they just have to give the judge a reason to vote against the plan. They get speeches 2, 4, 5, and 7 (two of theirs come back-to-back — that's the NEG block).
terms.example: Against a Medicare for All AFF, the NEG might argue it will bankrupt the country, that a public option would be better, or that the AFF's evidence is wrong about how bad the current system is.
terms.where: NEG speaks second (1NC) and gets to close the middle of the round with the NEG block.
terms.watch: Being 'negative' doesn't mean being negative about everything — pick your best arguments and go hard. Trying to win on ten arguments usually loses to trying to win on two.

terms.def: Your one teammate. You debate together as a team — two of you versus two of them.
terms.plain: Your partner splits the speeches with you. One of you handles the first speeches of the round, the other handles the later ones. You share prep time, share a flow, and share the win or loss on the ballot.
terms.example: If you give the 1AC and the 2AC, your partner gives the 1AR and the 2AR. You split cross-examinations too.
terms.where: Every speech, every CX, every prep-time huddle.
terms.watch: During your partner's speech, don't sit there frozen — flow, prep answers, and pass notes. The round doesn't pause when it's not your turn.

terms.def: The whole debate event from start to finish, which usually takes about 90 minutes.
terms.plain: A round is one complete debate: eight speeches, four cross-examinations, and prep time in between, all judged by one adult. You'll usually debate 4–6 rounds at a tournament.
terms.example: Round 1 at a Saturday tournament might start at 8:30 AM and end around 10:00 AM, with the judge disclosing the winner right after (or later online).
terms.where: The whole event — from the judge saying "start when ready" to the final ballot.
terms.watch: Don't check out after your last speech. The round isn't over until the judge decides — and judges often decide during those last minutes.

terms.def: The adult in the room who listens to both teams and decides who won.
terms.plain: The judge is the person you're actually debating for. They flow the round, evaluate the arguments, and pick a winner. Judges have different backgrounds — some are experienced debate coaches ("flow judges"), some are parents or community members ("lay judges") — and good debaters adapt their style to fit.
terms.example: A flow judge might follow rapid-fire technical debate. A parent judge needs you to slow down and explain what "DA" stands for.
terms.where: Sitting at the back or side of the room the whole round.
terms.watch: Talk to the judge, not the other team. Eye contact and clear signposting change how the ballot goes.

terms.def: The paper (or online form) where the judge writes down who won and why.
terms.plain: The ballot is the official record of the round. The judge marks which team won, gives each debater speaker points, and usually writes a comment (a "Reason for Decision") explaining why they voted the way they did. Reading your ballots after a tournament is one of the fastest ways to improve.
terms.example: "AFF wins. The NEG dropped the Solvency Turn on the second advantage, and the judge extended it through the 2AR."
terms.where: Filled out during and right after the round.
terms.watch: Ballots aren't personal attacks. Even harsh feedback is a gift — read every one.

terms.def: A whole day (or weekend) of debate rounds against different schools.
terms.plain: A tournament packs several rounds into one event. You'll usually get 4–6 preliminary rounds where you switch sides (AFF, then NEG, then AFF…). The best records advance to elimination rounds — single-loss brackets that end with one winning team.
terms.example: A Saturday novice tournament might run four rounds, hand out awards at the end of the day, and send the top four teams to a final round.
terms.where: Held at schools, colleges, or convention centers, usually on weekends.
terms.watch: Bring water, snacks, chargers, and paper. Tournaments are long. Rounds run late. Pack for the day.

terms.def: A debater who is new to policy debate, usually in their first year.
terms.plain: Novice is the beginner division — you'll only debate other novices. The arguments are usually simpler, the pace is slower, and judges expect clear speaking instead of technical jargon. It's designed so you can learn without getting steamrolled by experienced debaters.
terms.example: A novice AFF might read a simple three-contention case and defend it. A varsity AFF might read seven contentions at 300 words per minute.
terms.where: Novice divisions exist at almost every tournament.
terms.watch: Don't try to sound like a varsity debater. Judges reward clarity from novices way more than they reward speed.

terms.def: A timed turn where one debater talks while everyone else listens.
terms.plain: Every round has eight speeches, split evenly between the two teams. Each speech has a strict time limit — when the timer goes off, you stop. During a speech, the other team can't interrupt (that happens in CX).
terms.example: The 1AC is 8 minutes long. The 1AR is only 5. Managing time inside a speech is half the skill.
terms.where: All eight of them, back-to-back with prep time and CX in between.
terms.watch: Rambling burns your speech time. Write the first 30 seconds of every speech ahead of time.

terms.def: Your first speech, where you build your main arguments and read your evidence.
terms.plain: There are four constructive speeches in a round: 1AC, 1NC, 2AC, and 2NC. Constructives are 8 minutes each, and they're the only speeches where you can introduce brand-new arguments. After the constructives are over, you can only extend and explain what's already on the flow.
terms.example: The 1NC is where the NEG reads their disadvantages, counterplan, and topicality — all fresh arguments the AFF hasn't heard yet.
terms.where: Speeches 1, 2, 3, and 4 of the round.
terms.watch: New arguments in rebuttals get thrown out. If you don't say it in a constructive, you probably can't say it later.

terms.def: Your second speech, where you respond to the other team and explain why you should win.
terms.plain: Rebuttals are the last four speeches of the round: 1NR, 1AR, 2NR, 2AR. They're only 5 minutes each. You can't introduce new arguments — you can only extend, answer, and weigh what's already been said. This is where the round is actually decided.
terms.example: The 2NR picks the two or three arguments the NEG wants to win on and buries them in weighing. Everything else gets kicked (dropped).
terms.where: Speeches 5, 6, 7, and 8 of the round.
terms.watch: Rebuttals aren't for reading new evidence — they're for explaining why what's already there wins the round.

terms.def: A 3-minute chunk of time where you ask the other team questions and they have to answer.
terms.plain: After each of the four constructive speeches, the debater who did NOT just give the speech gets 3 minutes to question the debater who did. CX is for four things: clarifying ("what did you mean?"), investigating ("where's your evidence?"), setting up ("getting them to admit something you'll use later"), and highlighting flaws ("making the judge notice a weakness").
terms.example: AFF in CX to NEG: "Your disadvantage says the economy is doing great right now — but your evidence is from 2019. Do you have anything newer?"
terms.where: After each constructive: four total CX periods per round.
terms.watch: CX is not for embarrassing the other team. Judges hate that. Ask questions that set up your NEXT speech.

terms.def: A shared bank of minutes you and your partner can use to think before any of your speeches.
terms.plain: Each team gets a total of 5–8 minutes (depends on the tournament) of prep time for the WHOLE round. You can use it however you want — 30 seconds here, 2 minutes there. When it's gone, it's gone. Managing it is a strategy skill.
terms.example: The AFF might burn 3 minutes of prep before the 2AC (because there's so much to answer) and save the rest for the 1AR.
terms.where: Between speeches — you announce "AFF taking prep" and start the clock.
terms.watch: Novices burn all their prep before the 2AC and have nothing left for the 1AR — the hardest speech of the round. Save some.

terms.def: The very first speech. The AFF reads their plan and case.
terms.plain: The 1AC is 8 minutes long and it's the ONE speech in the round that's written ahead of time. The AFF reads their plan text, their contentions (usually one for the problem and one or two for the advantages), and all the evidence that backs them up.
terms.example: A Medicare for All 1AC would read the plan text, then Contention 1 (millions of Americans are uninsured), Contention 2 (M4A saves lives), and Contention 3 (M4A is affordable).
terms.where: Speech 1 of 8.
terms.watch: Practice reading the 1AC out loud until you can hit the 8-minute mark without going over or leaving 90 seconds on the clock.

terms.def: The NEG's first speech. They attack the AFF and read new arguments.
terms.plain: The 1NC is where the NEG unloads. In 8 minutes, they usually read a disadvantage or two, maybe a counterplan or kritik, sometimes a topicality argument, and then attack the AFF's case directly (on-case). It's the widest speech of the round.
terms.example: A 1NC might read: 1 T-shell ("the AFF isn't topical"), 1 DA ("the plan crashes the economy"), 1 CP ("states should do it instead"), and 5 on-case answers.
terms.where: Speech 2 of 8, right after CX of the 1AC.
terms.watch: Reading too many arguments (a "wide 1NC") sounds impressive but leaves you no time to WIN any of them later. Fewer, deeper arguments beat more, shallower ones.

terms.def: The AFF's second speech. They answer everything the NEG said.
terms.plain: The 2AC has to answer EVERY argument the NEG made in the 1NC — no drops. In 8 minutes, that means quick, focused responses on each flow: 3–5 answers per off-case argument, plus rebuilding the case where the NEG attacked. It's a busy speech.
terms.example: "On the T-shell: 1) We meet, 2) Counter-interp, 3) Reasonable interpretations should be preferred. On the DA: 1) No link, 2) No uniqueness, 3) Turn — the plan HELPS the economy…"
terms.where: Speech 3 of 8.
terms.watch: One dropped 1NC argument becomes a free NEG win in the block. Answer everything, even if the answer is short.

terms.def: The NEG's second speech. Start of the NEG block.
terms.plain: The 2NC is the first half of the NEG block — two back-to-back NEG speeches (2NC + 1NR) with no AFF speech in between. The 2NC and 1NR usually split up the arguments: one takes the DA and CP, the other takes case and topicality. Together they're 13 minutes of NEG.
terms.example: "2NC will take the DA and the CP. 1NR will take case and T."
terms.where: Speech 4 of 8.
terms.watch: Don't repeat what your partner will say in the 1NR — split the arguments cleanly at the start of the block.

terms.def: The NEG's third speech. Second half of the NEG block.
terms.plain: The 1NR follows the 2NC immediately, with no AFF speech in between. It's 5 minutes. Together with the 2NC, that's 13 minutes of NEG the AFF has to answer in the 1AR (5 minutes). This is why the block is so brutal for the AFF.
terms.example: If the 2NC took the DA, the 1NR takes case: extending on-case attacks, adding depth to arguments the 2AC didn't answer well.
terms.where: Speech 5 of 8.
terms.watch: Even though the 1NR feels like a follow-up, it's still a full speech. Signpost carefully — the AFF is trying to figure out where you are on the flow so they can answer.

terms.def: The AFF's hardest speech. They answer the whole NEG block by themselves.
terms.plain: The 1AR gets 5 minutes to answer 13 minutes of NEG (the 2NC + 1NR). Every serious 1AR-er picks their battles: they extend the arguments they'll win on, group multiple weak NEG points into one quick answer, and let unimportant stuff die. Widely considered the toughest speech in policy debate.
terms.example: "Group the top 3 DA answers: even if the link is true, there's no impact — extend our impact defense. On the CP…"
terms.where: Speech 6 of 8.
terms.watch: You can't answer everything in 5 minutes. Trying to will make every answer too shallow. Pick your winners.

terms.def: The NEG's last speech. They pick the arguments they want to win on.
terms.plain: The 2NR is 5 minutes. This is where the NEG collapses the round — they kick (drop) the arguments they're losing and go all-in on their best one or two. The 2NR is a strategic speech: it's about choosing what to fight for, not covering everything.
terms.example: "We're going for the DA. Kick the CP, kick T, extend the DA and weigh it against case."
terms.where: Speech 7 of 8, right before the AFF's last speech.
terms.watch: Trying to go for everything in the 2NR usually means going for nothing well. Pick your winner and commit.

terms.def: The AFF's last speech. Final chance to explain why they win.
terms.plain: The 2AR is 5 minutes, and it's the last thing the judge hears. Like the 2NR, it should collapse: extend the AFF's best 1–2 arguments, weigh them against the NEG's best, and paint a clear picture of why the plan wins the round. No new arguments — but you can (and should) do heavy weighing.
terms.example: "Extend our Solvency Turn on the DA and the case impact. Compare: our advantage saves millions of lives, their DA is speculative. Vote AFF."
terms.where: Speech 8 of 8 — the last word of the round.
terms.watch: The 2AR is not the time to answer things the 1AR forgot. It IS the time to weigh, weigh, weigh.

terms.def: A quote from an article, book, or expert that backs up what you're saying.
terms.plain: Evidence is what separates policy debate from a regular argument. You don't just SAY the plan works — you quote a professor, a doctor, a policy expert who says it works. Every major argument in a round should be supported by a card.
terms.example: "Our evidence from Dr. Chen, health economist at Yale, 2025, says Medicare for All would save $450 billion per year."
terms.where: Read during constructive speeches, referenced ("extended") in rebuttals.
terms.watch: Just reading a card isn't enough — you have to explain what it says and why it matters. Judges don't reward evidence they don't understand.

terms.def: A single piece of evidence, with a tag, the author's name, and the quote itself.
terms.plain: A card is a three-part unit: (1) the TAG, a one-sentence summary of what the card proves; (2) the CITE, telling you who wrote it and when; and (3) the BODY, the actual quote from the source. In files, cards are stacked one after another.
terms.example: TAG: Medicare for All saves lives. CITE: Chen, Yale, 2025. BODY: "A single-payer system would prevent an estimated 68,000 deaths per year in the United States by expanding access to preventive care…"
terms.where: Everywhere in a case, a DA, a CP — anywhere an argument needs backup.
terms.watch: A card without a good tag is useless in a round. You'll never find it in time if the tag doesn't tell you what's inside.

terms.def: The one-sentence summary written above a card so you know what it proves.
terms.plain: The tag is the first thing you say when you read a card out loud. It's a short, active-voice claim, usually under 20 words. A good tag lets the judge know exactly what the card proves before they hear a single word of the quote.
terms.example: GOOD TAG: "Medicare for All saves 68,000 lives per year." WEAK TAG: "This card is about healthcare."
terms.where: Written directly above every card in the file.
terms.watch: Writing tags is a skill — don't outsource it to AI. If you can't summarize the card in one sentence, you don't understand what it says.

terms.def: The author's name, their job, and the date of the article the card comes from.
terms.plain: The cite tells the judge (and the other team) where a card came from. It usually includes the author's name, their qualifications (job title, university), the year, and sometimes the publication. A strong cite makes evidence more believable.
terms.example: "Chen, Professor of Health Economics at Yale University, 2025, published in the New England Journal of Medicine."
terms.where: Read out loud right after the tag, before the body of the card.
terms.watch: "Chen 2025" alone isn't enough. Say the qual — the judge won't know Chen is an economist unless you tell them.

terms.def: Marking the exact words in a card that you'll read out loud in the speech.
terms.plain: A source article might be 3,000 words long — but you only have time to read a few sentences. Highlighting is how you mark (usually with a colored underline or highlight in the doc) the specific words you'll actually say. The un-highlighted parts still count as evidence — the other team can quote from them in CX or their next speech.
terms.example: A 400-word block of text with 40 highlighted words scattered through it. Those 40 words are what gets read; the rest is context.
terms.where: Done ahead of the round when you're prepping cards.
terms.watch: Under-highlighting can make your card say something the author didn't mean. Highlight for meaning, not for speed.

terms.def: Your big idea (the top bread of the argument sandwich).
terms.plain: The Claim is your destination — the main point you're trying to make. It's the tagline of the argument. If someone asked you "what are you saying?" the Claim is the one-sentence answer.
terms.example: "Medicare for All saves lives." That's a claim. It's your destination — now you need fuel (a warrant) and a reason it matters (an impact).
terms.where: The first thing you say when you make an argument. Also the first thing you write on your flow.
terms.watch: A claim by itself isn't an argument. Anyone can claim anything. It only becomes an argument when you back it up with a warrant.

terms.def: Your reason or evidence (the filling of the sandwich).
terms.plain: The Warrant is your fuel — the reason your claim is true. It's the "why." It could be evidence from a card, a logical explanation, or an example. Without a warrant, a claim is just an opinion.
terms.example: Claim: "Medicare for All saves lives." Warrant: "Because when people have insurance, they see doctors earlier and catch diseases before they become deadly — Dr. Chen 2025."
terms.where: Follows the claim, either as evidence or as your own reasoning.
terms.watch: "Because that's just true" is not a warrant. Neither is "because everyone knows." Warrants have to actually explain something.

terms.def: Why your idea matters (the bottom bread of the sandwich).
terms.plain: The Impact is your mission success — the reason the judge should care. It answers "so what?" A great claim with a great warrant still loses if there's no impact. Impacts are usually about lives, money, freedom, the environment — big stakes.
terms.example: Claim + Warrant: "M4A saves lives because coverage means earlier care (Chen 2025)." Impact: "That's 68,000 fewer American deaths every year."
terms.where: The last part of every argument. Extended and weighed in every rebuttal.
terms.watch: "That's bad" isn't an impact. Get specific: how bad? How many people? How likely?

terms.def: A complete idea with a claim, a warrant, and an impact. All three parts together.
terms.plain: An argument is a sandwich: Claim on top (your main point), Warrant in the middle (your reason), Impact on the bottom (why it matters). If you're missing a piece, it's not an argument — it's just a statement. The judge won't vote for an incomplete argument.
terms.example: "The plan crashes the economy (claim) because it costs $3 trillion (warrant), which triggers a recession that costs 5 million jobs (impact)."
terms.where: Every position in the round is built out of arguments.
terms.watch: If the other team drops your claim but you never gave a warrant or impact, you didn't win anything.

terms.def: The part of an argument that connects the AFF's plan to a bad (or good) result.
terms.plain: The link says "the plan CAUSES this thing." In a disadvantage, the link is what connects the AFF's plan to the bad outcome. Without a link, a DA is just a story about something bad — it has nothing to do with the AFF.
terms.example: DA claim: "M4A crashes the economy." Link: "M4A costs $3 trillion, and government spending that high triggers inflation."
terms.where: Read in the 1NC as part of every DA and most CPs.
terms.watch: A weak link is the easiest place for the AFF to attack. "No link" is one of the strongest 2AC answers.

terms.def: The part of an argument that says something is (or isn't) already happening right now.
terms.plain: Uniqueness is the "before-the-plan" snapshot. A DA needs uniqueness to prove the bad thing hasn't already happened. If the economy is already crashing, then the AFF plan can't cause an economic crash — that impact is "non-unique."
terms.example: DA uniqueness: "The economy is strong right now — GDP is growing 3.2% this quarter." Then the link explains why the plan RUINS that.
terms.where: Almost always the first card read in a 1NC disadvantage.
terms.watch: "Non-unique" is a fast 2AC answer: if the bad thing is already happening, the plan can't cause it.

terms.def: The step-by-step chain that shows how one thing leads to another.
terms.plain: Internal links are the middle pieces of an argument's chain. If a DA says "the plan causes X, which causes Y, which causes Z, which is bad," the middle steps are internal links. The more steps in the chain, the easier it is for the AFF to break one.
terms.example: "M4A → higher government spending → inflation → dollar collapses → global recession → nuclear war." Every arrow is an internal link that needs evidence.
terms.where: In DAs, advantages, kritiks — anywhere a chain of consequences is claimed.
terms.watch: A chain is only as strong as its weakest link. AFFs win by proving ONE internal link is broken.

terms.def: The Affirmative team's specific policy proposal or solution to a problem.
terms.plain: The plan is the AFF's actual proposal — a specific policy change, written out in a sentence or two. Everything the AFF defends comes back to their plan. The NEG can't attack a plan that wasn't proposed, and the AFF can't defend one they didn't read.
terms.example: PLAN TEXT: "The United States federal government should establish national health insurance modeled on the Medicare for All Act of 2023."
terms.where: Read as part of the 1AC, usually right after the introduction and before the contentions.
terms.watch: Write the plan text carefully. Every word can be attacked in a Topicality debate. Vague plans lose to precise ones.

terms.def: How big the problem is.
terms.plain: Significance is one of the four "stock issues" of the AFF case. It answers the question: is this problem big enough to be worth doing something about? A case with tiny significance won't outweigh even a small disadvantage.
terms.example: "29 million Americans are uninsured. 68,000 people die each year from lack of coverage. This is a massive problem."
terms.where: Established in the 1AC, usually inside a Contention.
terms.watch: "It's bad" isn't significance. Give numbers, scale, and human stakes.

terms.def: Who is being hurt by the problem right now.
terms.plain: Harms is one of the four stock issues. It answers: who suffers because the status quo is broken? Harms make the round emotional — real people, real damage. They give the judge someone to care about.
terms.example: "Sarah, a 34-year-old cancer patient without insurance, delayed treatment for months and died from a curable illness. Millions face this."
terms.where: Told as part of the case in the 1AC.
terms.watch: Statistics can numb the judge. Pair numbers with specific stories.

terms.def: Why the problem isn't fixed already.
terms.plain: Inherency is the "barrier" argument. Something must be stopping the fix from happening right now — otherwise the plan wouldn't be needed. Usually the barrier is political (Congress won't pass it), structural (the current system won't allow it), or economic (nobody's willing to pay).
terms.example: "Insurance companies spend billions lobbying against reform. Every serious M4A bill has died in committee because of this. Only the plan can break through."
terms.where: Established in the 1AC, sometimes as its own contention.
terms.watch: If the NEG proves the plan is already happening (or about to), your inherency is dead and so is your case.

terms.def: Whether or not your plan actually works to fix the problem.
terms.plain: Solvency is one of the four stock issues, and it's the one the NEG will attack the hardest. It answers: does the plan actually solve? An AFF can have huge significance, awful harms, and clear inherency — but if the plan doesn't solve, they lose.
terms.example: "Countries with single-payer systems have 30% lower per-capita healthcare costs and better outcomes. The plan gets us those results."
terms.where: Argued in the 1AC and rebuilt throughout the round when the NEG attacks it.
terms.watch: "Solvency Take-Outs" — arguments that the plan won't work — are one of the NEG's most common weapons. Have answers ready.

terms.def: Everything the AFF reads in their first speech (plan + all the reasons it's a good idea).
terms.plain: "Case" is a catch-all term for the AFF's whole 1AC: the plan text plus all the contentions and advantages. When the NEG attacks "on case," they're attacking the arguments inside the AFF's 1AC directly, instead of running new NEG positions.
terms.example: "The 2NR will go for on-case — the AFF's inherency evidence is from 2019 and their solvency card doesn't even mention the plan."
terms.where: Read in the 1AC, defended for the rest of the round.
terms.watch: AFFs often ignore case in later speeches to focus on off-case attacks. Don't. If your case dies, your whole round dies.

terms.def: One big section of the AFF case, usually one advantage.
terms.plain: The case is broken into contentions — labeled sections like "Contention 1: Inherency" or "Contention 2: The Coverage Advantage." Each contention makes one major argument and has its own evidence. Most novice cases have 2–3 contentions.
terms.example: "Contention 1: The healthcare system is broken. Contention 2: M4A solves. Contention 3: The economy benefits."
terms.where: The 1AC, and referenced throughout the round.
terms.watch: Announce your contentions clearly ("Now on Contention 2…"). Judges rely on this to keep their flow organized.

terms.def: A good thing that will happen if the AFF's plan passes.
terms.plain: An advantage is the AFF's reason to vote for the plan. Each advantage has its own uniqueness ("this problem is happening now"), link ("the plan fixes it"), and impact ("the fix matters this much"). Most cases have 1–3 advantages.
terms.example: "Advantage 1: Lives. M4A saves 68,000 Americans per year from preventable death."
terms.where: Part of the case, read in the 1AC.
terms.watch: Big impacts ("prevents nuclear war") sound impressive but are hard to defend. Novices win more with grounded, believable impacts ("saves lives, saves money").

terms.def: The way things are right now, before the AFF's plan.
terms.plain: The status quo is the current state of the world — the baseline. The AFF argues the status quo is broken and needs the plan. The NEG often defends the status quo, arguing things are fine, or at least better than what the plan would do.
terms.example: "In the status quo, 29 million Americans have no health insurance. That's what we're changing."
terms.where: Referenced throughout the round, especially in inherency and disadvantage debates.
terms.watch: "Status quo solves" is a classic NEG argument — that the current system is already fixing the problem. AFFs need answers.

terms.def: Attacking the Affirmative team's evidence directly.
terms.plain: On-case arguments attack the AFF where they LIVE — inside the AFF's own case. That means challenging the significance ("it's not that big a problem"), inherency ("it's already being fixed"), or solvency ("the plan won't work"). On-case doesn't bring in new outside arguments — it dismantles the ones the AFF already made.
terms.example: "On the AFF's second advantage — their solvency evidence is from 2018. Newer studies show single-payer costs MORE, not less. Their whole advantage is outdated."
terms.where: Read in the 1NC after all the off-case, extended in the block.
terms.watch: Novices often skip on-case to focus on "cool" DAs. Bad move — an AFF with no case defense usually still wins if you can't prove the plan is worse than the status quo.

terms.def: Bringing up totally new reasons why the Affirmative's plan will fail.
terms.plain: Off-case arguments are positions the NEG brings in that aren't a direct attack on the case — they're new arguments the AFF didn't see coming. The main off-case types are Disadvantages (DAs), Counterplans (CPs), Kritiks (Ks), and Topicality (T). A typical 1NC has 2–4 off-case positions.
terms.example: "1NC will be: T-shell, one DA (economy), and one CP (states)."
terms.where: Read at the top of the 1NC, before on-case attacks.
terms.watch: Reading too many off-case positions ("a wide 1NC") means you can't win any of them well. 2–3 solid positions beat 5 shallow ones.

terms.def: An argument that the Affirmative's plan will cause terrible new side effects, making things worse.
terms.plain: A DA has four parts: Uniqueness (things are stable now), Link (the plan disrupts them), Internal Link (the disruption causes something bad), and Impact (the bad thing matters). If any part is missing, the DA doesn't function. The NEG's job is to prove the plan makes the world worse than the status quo.
terms.example: "Economy DA: 1) Economy is strong now (uniqueness). 2) M4A costs $3 trillion (link). 3) That triggers inflation (internal link). 4) Inflation causes global recession — millions unemployed (impact)."
terms.where: Read in the 1NC as an off-case position.
terms.watch: The AFF will attack the weakest link in your DA chain. Make sure every step has solid evidence.

terms.def: When the Negative team gets to give two back-to-back speeches without the Affirmative interrupting.
terms.plain: The NEG Block is the 2NC + 1NR — 13 straight minutes of NEG (with a CX in the middle) before the AFF speaks again. It's the biggest structural advantage the NEG has. Good NEG teams split arguments cleanly between the two speeches to maximize coverage.
terms.example: "2NC takes the DA and the CP. 1NR takes case and T. Split the block, no double-covering."
terms.where: Speeches 4 and 5 of the round.
terms.watch: AFFs sometimes forget to prep during the block because they're overwhelmed. Big mistake — the 1AR needs every second of prep you can find.

terms.def: A different plan the NEG offers that solves the problem better than the AFF's.
terms.plain: A CP is the NEG saying: "We agree the problem is real — but our plan is better than theirs." To win, the CP has to solve the AFF's harms AND avoid a disadvantage the AFF's plan causes. The NEG has to prove their plan is BETTER, not just different.
terms.example: AFF: "Federal government does M4A." NEG CP: "States do M4A instead. Solves the harms AND avoids the federalism DA."
terms.where: Read in the 1NC as an off-case position, often paired with a DA the CP avoids.
terms.watch: A CP that does the same thing as the AFF isn't a counterplan — it's just agreeing with them. There has to be a real difference ("net benefit") the CP provides.

terms.def: An argument that the AFF's whole way of thinking about the problem is wrong.
terms.plain: A kritik (spelled with a K, from German) is a philosophical criticism. Instead of debating the plan's effects, the K argues that the AFF's assumptions, language, or worldview are harmful. Kritiks are usually seen in varsity rounds, not novice — they can get complicated fast.
terms.example: "Cap K: The AFF's plan tries to fix healthcare inside capitalism, which is the root cause of health inequality. Voting AFF entrenches the very system causing the harm."
terms.where: Read in the 1NC as an off-case position. Rare at the novice level.
terms.watch: Kritiks require deep understanding of the philosophy behind them. Don't read a K you can't explain in plain English.

terms.def: An attack that says the AFF's plan won't actually work.
terms.plain: A solvency take-out is an on-case argument that directly attacks whether the AFF's plan solves the problem. Even if the harms are real and the plan is a good idea in theory, if the plan doesn't actually work, the AFF loses. Take-outs make the plan's benefits go to zero.
terms.example: "Solvency take-out: Their evidence is about single-payer in Canada — a country of 40 million. The U.S. has 335 million people. It doesn't scale."
terms.where: Read as part of on-case in the 1NC.
terms.watch: One solvency take-out with strong evidence is often more valuable than three weak DAs. Judges love a well-executed take-out.

terms.def: Flipping the other team's argument so it becomes a reason to vote for YOU.
terms.plain: A turn takes the other team's argument and reverses it. Instead of just answering "you're wrong," you say "you're wrong AND the opposite is a reason I win." There are two kinds: Link Turns (the plan does the opposite of what you claim) and Impact Turns (the thing you say is bad is actually good).
terms.example: NEG DA: "M4A hurts the economy." AFF Impact Turn: "Even if it does, the economic slowdown would reduce carbon emissions — good for climate."
terms.where: Read in the speech right after the argument you're turning.
terms.watch: NEVER turn the LINK and the IMPACT at the same time. If you say the plan doesn't hurt the economy (link turn) AND hurting the economy is good (impact turn), you've contradicted yourself. The other team will call you out.

terms.def: Saying the "bad thing" the other team is worried about is actually good.
terms.plain: An impact turn agrees that the plan causes X — but argues X is a GOOD thing. It's a bold move because it commits you to defending something everyone assumed was bad. Done well, it wins rounds. Done poorly, it looks ridiculous.
terms.example: NEG DA: "M4A causes government spending → inflation." AFF Impact Turn: "Actually, a little inflation is good — it means wages rise. Extend our economics card."
terms.where: Made in the 2AC (against a 1NC DA) or wherever the argument first appears.
terms.watch: You CANNOT turn the link AND the impact together — that's a contradiction. Pick one or the other.

terms.def: Saying the AFF's plan does the opposite of what the NEG claims.
terms.plain: A link turn attacks the link of a DA. Instead of just saying "no link," it says "the plan actually does the OPPOSITE — and that's a reason to vote for us." So instead of the plan causing the bad thing, the plan PREVENTS the bad thing.
terms.example: NEG: "M4A tanks the economy." AFF Link Turn: "M4A actually BOOSTS the economy — freeing families from medical debt gives them money to spend."
terms.where: Made in the 2AC against 1NC disadvantages.
terms.watch: You CANNOT turn the link AND the impact at the same time. Pick one. Doing both = contradiction = the NEG collects the turn against YOU.

terms.def: An argument that says the Affirmative's plan doesn't match the resolution, which is like calling them out for breaking the rules of the game.
terms.plain: Topicality is a NEG argument that the AFF's plan isn't actually about the resolution. It has three parts: (1) a Definition of a key word in the resolution, (2) an Interpretation of what the resolution requires, and (3) a Violation showing the AFF broke the interpretation. If the NEG wins T, the AFF loses no matter how good their case is.
terms.example: Resolution says "establish national health insurance." NEG T: "'National' means federal-level. The AFF's plan is state-run. They're not topical — vote NEG."
terms.where: Read in the 1NC as an off-case position, often first.
terms.watch: T is a stock argument at every level. AFFs need a prepared "We Meet" and "Counter-Interpretation" for common T-violations on the topic.

terms.def: What a word in the resolution actually means. Both teams argue over these.
terms.plain: Definitions are the raw material of Topicality debates. The NEG reads a definition of a key word (usually from a dictionary or an academic source) that excludes the AFF's plan. The AFF reads their own definition that INCLUDES the plan. The judge picks whichever definition is better supported.
terms.example: NEG: "'National' means acting at the federal level (Merriam-Webster)." AFF: "'National' means throughout the country, which state-by-state adoption satisfies (Black's Law Dictionary)."
terms.where: Read as part of a T-shell in the 1NC, answered in the 2AC.
terms.watch: Definitions from field-specific sources (medical journals, policy think tanks) usually beat generic dictionaries.

terms.def: Your team's version of what a word in the resolution means.
terms.plain: An interpretation is a team's proposed rule for what the resolution requires. The NEG's interpretation excludes the AFF's plan; the AFF's counter-interpretation includes it. Judges usually pick the interpretation that leads to "better debates" — more predictable, more educational, more fair.
terms.example: NEG Interp: "The AFF must establish a single-payer system." AFF Counter-Interp: "The AFF must establish any form of universal coverage, including public options."
terms.where: Read as part of the T-shell (NEG) or the 2AC's answers (AFF).
terms.watch: "Our interp is better because…" is where the T debate is actually won or lost. Have standards ready: predictability, ground, education.

terms.def: The NEG saying the AFF broke their interpretation of the resolution.
terms.plain: The violation is where the NEG proves the AFF's plan doesn't fit the NEG's interpretation. It's the specific step that says "the AFF is doing X, which our interpretation doesn't allow." AFFs answer with "We Meet" — proving they actually DO fit the interpretation.
terms.example: "Our interpretation: 'national' means federal. Violation: The AFF's plan hands the program to state governments — they don't establish anything national."
terms.where: Third part of a T-shell, right after definition and interpretation.
terms.watch: "We Meet" is the AFF's fastest way to beat a T argument. Get comfortable with this move.

terms.def: A special kind of debate note-taking done on a piece of paper turned sideways to track arguments.
terms.plain: Flowing is how you track every argument through every speech. Turn your paper sideways (landscape). Draw 8 columns — one per speech. As each side speaks, write short abbreviations of their arguments in the right column, then draw arrows showing how arguments get answered (or don't). By the end of the round, your flow shows exactly what happened.
terms.example: Column 1 = 1AC arguments. Column 2 = 1NC answers. Column 3 = 2AC answers to those. Arrows connect answers to what they're answering.
terms.where: Every speech, every round, without exception.
terms.watch: Use abbreviations. "w/o" for without, "b/c" for because, ✓ for answered, ✗ for dropped. If you try to write full words, you'll fall behind.

terms.def: An argument that a team forgot to answer. In debate, an unanswered argument is treated as true by the judge.
terms.plain: A drop is HUGE. If the AFF says something in the 2AC and the NEG doesn't answer it in the 2NC or 1NR, it's a drop — and the judge treats it as true, even if it's a wild claim. Finding drops on the flow and pointing them out is one of the most powerful moves in debate.
terms.example: "They dropped our impact turn on the DA. Extend it — that means their disadvantage now HELPS us."
terms.where: Called out in rebuttals, especially the 2NR and 2AR.
terms.watch: Cover everything. Even a bad answer beats no answer. Silence = the argument wins.

terms.def: Looking at your flow notes and answering your opponent's arguments one by one, in order.
terms.plain: Line-by-line is a style of refutation: go down the flow, point by point, and answer each argument in the same order the other team made them. It makes your speech easy for the judge to follow (they're flowing the same way you are).
terms.example: "On their first answer, group 1 and 2 — both wrong because of our Chen card. On their third answer, our evidence assumes their argument. On their fourth…"
terms.where: The main structure of every rebuttal.
terms.watch: Going out of order confuses the judge and makes the flow messy. Even if it feels slower, go down the flow in the order things appeared.

terms.def: Comparing your team's impact to the other team's impact to see which one is more likely, happens sooner, or affects more people.
terms.plain: Impact calculus (or "impact calc") is how you tell the judge which impact matters more. The three classic factors are: Probability (which is more likely to actually happen?), Timeframe (which happens sooner?), and Magnitude (which affects more people?). Sometimes called P-T-M.
terms.example: "Our impact outweighs on all three: Probability — our card is peer-reviewed. Timeframe — deaths from lack of coverage happen every day. Magnitude — 68,000 lives per year is bigger than their speculative recession."
terms.where: Every rebuttal, especially the 2NR and 2AR.
terms.watch: The team that does impact calc almost always wins. If both teams have impacts and neither compares them, the judge is stuck guessing.

terms.def: Your written notes of every argument in the round, laid out in columns.
terms.plain: "The flow" is the physical paper (or digital doc) where you track arguments. Each off-case position and the case each get their own flow (or their own section). By the end of the round, your flows show every argument, every answer, and every drop.
terms.example: "Flip to the DA flow — extend our uniqueness card, cross-apply to their link."
terms.where: Every debater has a flow for every speech, always.
terms.watch: Keep separate flows for separate arguments. Trying to fit the DA, CP, and T all on one page turns into chaos fast.

terms.def: Bringing an argument forward from an earlier speech into a later one.
terms.plain: To extend an argument means to pull it forward into the current speech and explain why it still matters. In rebuttals, you can't make new arguments — you can only extend ones already on the flow. "Extending" also means highlighting an argument the other team dropped.
terms.example: "Extend our economy DA — they dropped the link card, which means the DA is conceded. Now extend the impact: recession causes 5 million job losses."
terms.where: In every rebuttal.
terms.watch: Just SAYING "extend" isn't enough. Explain what the argument is and why it wins. Judges hate lazy extensions.

terms.def: Any response you give to the other team's argument.
terms.plain: An "answer" is a response to an argument on the flow. Answers can be short ("no link") or full arguments with their own evidence. Debaters number their answers ("1)... 2)... 3)…") so the flow stays clean and the judge can follow.
terms.example: "Three answers to the DA: 1) Non-unique — economy already falling. 2) No link — the plan doesn't affect spending. 3) Turn — plan boosts the economy."
terms.where: In every speech after the constructive that started the argument.
terms.watch: Two GOOD answers beat five bad ones. Judges will remember one strong response but forget five weak ones.

terms.def: Telling the judge exactly where you are on the flow ("Now on the DA…").
terms.plain: Signposting is saying out loud where you are before you argue. It sounds simple, but new debaters skip it and lose points. Every time you switch arguments, say something like "Now on the DA" or "Off the second contention." The judge relies on this to keep up.
terms.example: "That's it for topicality. Now off the DA. On their uniqueness card..."
terms.where: Constantly, throughout every speech.
terms.watch: Judges who lose track of where you are will drop arguments off their flow. If the judge misses it, you didn't say it.

terms.def: A quick preview at the start of your speech telling the judge the order you'll go in.
terms.plain: A roadmap is 5–15 seconds before your speech where you tell the judge what order you're covering things in. It doesn't count against your speech time. It lets the judge get their flows in the right order before you start.
terms.example: "Roadmap: I'll start with topicality, then the DA, then case. That work? Great — start when ready."
terms.where: At the very start of every speech, before the clock starts.
terms.watch: Don't put arguments IN your roadmap — just the order. "I'll go T, DA, case" is a roadmap. "I'll explain why T is a voter and…" is you burning speech time.

terms.def: A reason the judge should vote for your team.
terms.plain: A voter is an argument that, if you win it, means you win the round. Topicality voters are usually "fairness" and "education" — reasons the AFF's untopical plan hurts the debate. Impact voters are the big picture: "vote AFF because our advantage saves 68,000 lives, and their DA is speculative."
terms.example: "Two T voters: 1) Fairness — their plan destroys NEG ground. 2) Education — we learn nothing about the actual resolution. Both are voters."
terms.where: Called out in rebuttals, especially the 2NR and 2AR.
terms.watch: "Voter" is a magic word — use it. It signals to the judge that this is the KEY argument. Don't waste it on trivial stuff.

terms.def: Explaining why your arguments matter more than the other team's.
terms.plain: Weighing is comparison. It's not enough to have good arguments — you need to tell the judge why YOUR good arguments beat THEIR good arguments. The team that does more weighing usually wins, even when the arguments are equally strong.
terms.example: "Weigh our advantage against their DA: our impact is empirically proven (Canada, UK). Theirs is a speculative chain that requires FIVE internal links. Ours is more probable AND happens sooner."
terms.where: Every rebuttal, especially the 2NR and 2AR.
terms.watch: Weighing is the #1 skill that separates novice winners from novice losers. Do it early. Do it often.

terms.def: The rules the judge should use to decide who won.
terms.plain: Framework is the "how" of judging. It tells the judge what MATTERS. In a policy round, the standard framework is: the judge is a policymaker, and the team that shows their world is better wins. In kritik rounds, framework debates get complicated — teams argue over whether the judge should evaluate the plan's effects or the AFF's philosophy.
terms.example: "Framework: the judge should weigh consequences. The plan saves 68,000 lives. Vote AFF."
terms.where: Established (usually implicitly) in the 1AC. Debated explicitly when kritiks or Ts are in play.
terms.watch: In novice rounds, framework usually isn't contested — everyone assumes cost-benefit analysis. Don't overcomplicate it unless the other team forces you.

terms.def: A score (usually 1–30) the judge gives each debater for how well they spoke.
terms.plain: Speaker points (or "speaks") measure your individual performance in the round — separate from whether your team won. They're used to seed brackets and give out speaker awards. In novice, typical scores range from 26 to 29. A 30 is basically unheard of; anything below 25 usually means something went wrong.
terms.example: "You spoke clearly, signposted well, and did great weighing — 28.5 for you. Your partner rushed and dropped an argument — 27."
terms.where: Marked on the ballot after the round.
terms.watch: Speaker points reward clarity, organization, and respect. Being clever or sarcastic can lose you points fast — especially with lay judges.
